title: Where mindfulness came from
hookLine: mindfulness is in apps, offices and hospitals now; the word has a home in the early Buddhist teachings, and zen first meant meditation

cards: It's midnight, your brain won't stop, and you open an app. A calm voice says: let's practice mindfulness. At work there's a mindfulness workshop.
At the hospital, a mindfulness course for pain. The word is everywhere now, and it can sound brand new, like something invented in an office with good lighting. It isn't.
It has an address, and the address is about twenty-five centuries old. You've spent this week breathing. Before you build your own routine, let's say where it came from.

teach.b: First, the word. Mindfulness is an English choice for a word in Pali, the language of the early Buddhist teachings: sati. At its root, sati means remembering.

Remembering to come back to what's happening, right now. In 1881 the British scholar Thomas Rhys Davids, translating those teachings, used the word mindfulness for it, and it stuck. Second, the practice itself.

teach.h: BREATHING IN LONG, I KNOW IT.
teach.b: The early teachings describe a person sitting down, setting attention in front of them, and simply knowing: breathing in long, I know I'm breathing in long; breathing out short, I know I'm breathing out short.
That's mindfulness of breathing, and it's very close to what you did on day ninety-seven. Third, zen. The practice traveled east.
The Sanskrit word for meditation, dhyana, became chan in Chinese, seon in Korean, and zen in Japanese.

So zen, the word on candles and spa menus, first meant meditation, and it names a Buddhist school built around sitting. The counting you did three days ago comes from that world. Fourth, the hospital.
In 1979 Jon Kabat-Zinn started an eight-week course at a medical school in Massachusetts, Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction.
He drew it from Buddhist practice and taught it without the religious framework, so anyone could come. Buddhist teachers see that in different ways. Many are glad the practice reaches people in pain.
Some worry that a practice meant to free the mind from greed and harm can shrink into a productivity trick. Both views come from people who care about it. You don't have to settle it.
Just know whose practice it is.

how: Mindfulness of breathing is taught in Buddhist monasteries and in secular courses alike: attention rests on the breath, and each time it wanders, you remember and come back.

relaxing deeply until all stress melts away

practice: Settle, and from this week pick what fits you: just watching, a longer breath out, a double sigh, counting to ten, the box, or a plain word like here. Run through two or three of them now, gently, in the order you like.
When the mind wanders off, and it will, that's sati's moment: remember, and come back.

wordCard.voice: Sati, the Pali word English calls mindfulness: remembering to come back to what's happening now. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese chan, from Sanskrit dhyana, meditation; read zen in Japanese and seon in Korean.

carryVoice: Your line: remember, come back. Mindfulness has a home, and now you know the address. Day one hundred three.
